name: Musée National des Beaux-Arts d'Alger
watch: About 8,000 works, from Delacroix and Monet to Baya and Racim; reopened after its 2020 COVID closure.
records_note: It is a state establishment under the culture minister.

overview: National museum of fine arts in the Hamma district of Algiers, opposite the Jardin d'Essai, with about 8,000 works (Wikipedia, French Wikipedia).

It grew out of Algiers's municipal collections: a municipal museum opened in 1908 and closed in 1928, and a national museum of fine arts took over its collection. It was inaugurated on 5 May 1930 and opened to the public in April 1931, tied to the 1930 centenary of French presence in Algeria (modernism.ro, Lucian Muntean, 22 December 2024; Wikipedia).
Building: designed by architect Paul Guion, with work beginning in 1928 (Wikipedia). Funds from the 1930 centenary paid for 498 works in two years (Wikipedia).

Collection: paintings, prints, about 800 sculptures, about 2,000 numismatic pieces and decorative arts (French Wikipedia, Wikipedia). It includes the 1982 Mohamed Racim bequest of 61 works (French Wikipedia).

On 14 May 1962 more than 300 works were moved to the Louvre (modernism.ro). They were repatriated to Algeria by 1970 (Wikipedia). In November 1961, OAS commandos bombed a Bourdelle statue in the courtyard (Wikipedia).
Directors have included Jean Alazard (1930 to 1960), Jean de Maisonseul (1962 to 1975) and Malika Dorbani Bouabdellah (until 1994) (French Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: Musée National des Beaux-Arts d'Alger: national museum under Algerian state control
funding: Artessere describes it as a national institution that the 1962 Evian accords left under the control of the Algerian State.
Gifts: Sonatrach handed over 174 canvases by Juanita Guccione in 2012, and BNP Paribas gave two Étienne Dinet paintings in 2012 (French Wikipedia).
details.bottom_line: The museum is a national institution under Algerian state control. The documented private involvement is two gifts of artworks in 2012, from Sonatrach and BNP Paribas.

name: Fundação Sindika Dokolo
watch: Founders' fortune tied to Angolan state oil and diamond deals.
why_flagged: Founders' fortune tied to Angolan state oil and diamond deals.
records_note: The foundation's old domains are down or taken over.

overview: Cultural foundation headquartered in Luanda that looks after Sindika Dokolo's contemporary African art collection and ran the Luanda Triennial (Wikipedia).

Dokolo, a Congolese collector, began the collection in 2004 with the Angolan artist and curator Fernando Alvim and set up the foundation in 2006 (The Art Newspaper, 2017). Alvim was vice-president and Simon Njami a consultant (Wikipedia).

Named for its founder, the husband of Isabel dos Santos, daughter of former president José Eduardo dos Santos. He died free-diving off Dubai on 29 October 2020, aged 48, and Dubai Police found no criminal suspicion (Al Jazeera).

The collection began with the purchase of Hans Bogatzke's collection (Wikipedia) and held about 3,000 works by artists including William Kentridge, Zanele Muholi and Edson Chagas (The Art Newspaper, 2020).

Programmes: the Luanda Triennial, the Check List Luanda Pop side project at the 2007 Venice Biennale, a 2018 show with Documenta 14 artists it helped fund, and buying back looted works: in December 2015 it bought three Chokwe pieces from collectors in Belgium and France to return to the Dundo Museum (Wikipedia; The Art Newspaper).
details.funding_verdict: Fundação Sindika Dokolo: founder-funded: the Dokolo and dos Santos fortune
funding: The foundation paid for the Chokwe purchases itself, from collectors in Belgium and France, at prices the article does not disclose (The Art Newspaper, 2015).

In early January 2020 Angola froze the couple's assets and bank accounts; President João Lourenço sought to recover $1bn in state loans (The Art Newspaper). The Art Newspaper said it was not known whether the collection was targeted.

red_flags.heading: Founders' fortune from Angolan state deals
points: The ICIJ-led Luanda Leaks investigation, based on more than 715,000 documents, accused dos Santos of building her $2.2bn fortune through exploiting Angola; she denies that it came from nepotism and corruption (The Art Newspaper).
Her father appointed her head of the state oil company Sonangol in 2016; Lourenço fired her in 2017 (The Art Newspaper).

In July 2020 the Provincial Court of Luanda called the deal through which state diamond company Sodiam invested in the jeweller de Grisogono "fraudulent", saying it gave Dokolo and dos Santos the chance to control the company; Sodiam says it lost its $120 million investment (ICIJ). Dokolo's lawyers said he first invested $115 million and later much more.

red_flags.heading: US corruption designation
points: On 9 December 2021 the US State Department designated Isabel dos Santos for "significant corruption" and barred her and her immediate family from the United States (ICIJ).

press.overall: Little direct criticism found in art media; the one sustained attack is an opinion essay.

items.title: Carlos Salazar, "Alfredo Jaar, Muxima y los Dokolo de Angola, Resucitados" (2009)
points: Argues the collection's claim to dignify Africans is contradicted by the family's money: Dokolo's father's bank and its collapse in 1986, and diamond activity the author ties to abuses in the Lundas.

Faults Alfredo Jaar for never publicly distancing himself from Dokolo after showing in the 2007 African pavilion the collection organised, and quotes Barthélémy Toguo: "Under no circumstances whatever should my name be associated with that of Sindika Dokolo".
An openly polemical opinion piece; its allegations rest on press sources it cites.

items.title: Cristina Ruiz, "Africa's top collector returns ancestral works to Angola" (2015)
points: Not criticism: reports Dokolo's offer to repay collectors of stolen works only what they paid, and notes his marriage to the president's daughter.

details.bottom_line: The foundation ran on the private fortune of Dokolo and dos Santos, which Angolan courts, the ICIJ and the US government tie to state oil and diamond deals. No reporting found of activity since Dokolo's death in 2020, and its old domain now serves a gambling site. Worth watching: what Angolan or Portuguese courts decide about the collection.

name: HALLE FÜR KUNST Steiermark
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
highlight: A contemporary art exhibition house at Burgring 2 in Graz.

overview: Open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00, with free admission (e-flux directory, gallery website).

Formerly the Künstlerhaus Graz. Art associations began collecting money for a Künstlerhaus in 1903. The funds were confiscated after the 1938 Anschluss, and the building, designed by architect Robert Haueisen, opened on 20 June 1952 (German Wikipedia).
The Land Steiermark owns the building. Since January 2013 the Kunstverein Medienturm has run the house and set its programme (German Wikipedia).
From 2003 to 2012 the house was part of the Universalmuseum Joanneum, and it reopened as Halle für Kunst Steiermark in 2021 (German Wikipedia).
Sandro Droschl, head of the Kunstverein Medienturm, has led it since 2013 (e-flux directory). German Wikipedia says he won the selection process in 2012.
The building was renovated in 2010 to 2012 and again from 2020. The e-flux directory calls the early-1950s modernist pavilion one of the first white cubes in Austria.

Programme: solo and thematic group exhibitions, performances and residencies. The Trigon biennial ran there from 1963 to 1995 (e-flux directory, German Wikipedia). The 2026 to 2027 programme includes Katherine Bernhardt (24 September 2026 to 10 January 2027) and Josef Strau with Leroy Johnson (5 March to 9 May 2027) (gallery website).

In 2018 the Vereinigung Bildender Künstler Steiermark, the Sezession Graz and the Berufsvereinigung Bildender Künstler protested that their exhibition time had been cut from about half a year to 2.5 weeks for all associations together, and submitted 66 white canvases to a call for entries Droschl had issued (German Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: HALLE FÜR KUNST Steiermark: public: Land Steiermark, the Austrian federal government and the City of Graz
funding: Kronen Zeitung (krone.at), in an undated article by Christoph Hartner on the house's relaunch as Halle für Kunst Steiermark, reported that the Land raised the house's budget by €142,000 to €500,000, the federal government contributed €140,000 (40 percent more), and the City of Graz funding stayed at €102,000.
German Wikipedia says the building was constructed under the Land Steiermark as building client, with funds from the Land and the federal government; the Land remains its owner.
wider_context: "Heimatpflege-Notstand: Wie geht es nach dem steirischen Kultur-Eklat weiter?" (profil, Stefan Grissemann and Wolfgang Paterno, 22 March 2025; title translated: "Emergency in heritage care: what happens after the Styrian culture scandal?"): IG Kultur Steiermark's managing director Lidija Krienzer-Radojević said "Wir befinden uns in einer äußerst prekären Lage" (translated: "We are in an extremely precarious situation") and expected the current culture budget not to hold the 2024 funding level. Edith Draxl, former chair of the Kuratorium, gave funding sums of about €2.5 million in 2024 and €1.4 million in 2025, with cuts of 12 to 70 percent or rejections. Culture councillor Karlheinz Kornhäusl said the culture budget rose from just over €60 million in 2019 to about €81 million, with most going to large institutions.
The article does not name the Halle für Kunst. The Land Steiermark, whose culture budget it criticises, owns the building and pays €500,000 of the house's budget according to the Kronen Zeitung.
details.bottom_line: The Halle für Kunst Steiermark is a building owned by the Land Steiermark and run by an art association, paid for by the Land Steiermark, the Austrian federal government and the City of Graz. The Land's culture budget was criticised in profil in March 2025.

name: Haus Wittgenstein (Bulgarian Cultural Institute)
funding: The Bulgarian state bought the house in 1975 and runs it as the Bulgarian Cultural Institute, the embassy's cultural department. Both countries' culture ministries backed its 2024 Wittgenstein exhibition.
watch: Paul Engelmann and Ludwig Wittgenstein's house of 1928, a protected monument since 1971. It hosted a Wittgenstein exhibition in November 2024.
records_note: The house belongs to the Bulgarian state, which bought it in 1975.
affiliations_note: Owned by Bulgaria and run as the Bulgarian Cultural Institute within the Bulgarian Embassy's cultural department. Member of Iconic Houses.

overview: Villa at Kundmanngasse 19 (the institute's address is Parkgasse 18) in Vienna's 3rd district, Landstraße, near the U3 station Rochusgasse (Wien Geschichte Wiki, haus-wittgenstein.at).

Built for Margaret Stonborough-Wittgenstein, who gave Paul Engelmann the commission in 1926 according to the institute and in autumn 1925 according to the Wien Geschichte Wiki and English Wikipedia. Her brother Ludwig Wittgenstein joined the planning and, the institute says, became the sole architect. The house was finished in 1928.
Named for Ludwig Wittgenstein. English Wikipedia also calls it Stonborough House.

Three storeys with the main floor 1.5 metres above the ground, bare grey-white surfaces and a horizontal emphasis, on a plot with old chestnut trees that Stonborough chose over a family plot on Renngasse. Inside, the floors are terrazzo and the walls stuccolustro, and no reporting found of the structural materials (institute).

Bulgaria bought the house in 1975 with half the garden. The other half was built over with a 14-storey Hauptverband der Sozialversicherungsträger office block after protests by architects stopped the hotel high-rise planned by the building contractor Franz Katlein (Wien Geschichte Wiki, German Wikipedia).

Today it holds the Bulgarian Cultural Institute, the cultural department of the Bulgarian Embassy, with a parterre gallery and monthly exhibitions, concerts, readings and lectures (haus-wittgenstein.at).
Visiting: individual house tours are booked through the partner Architekturerbe Österreich and groups by email.
details.funding_verdict: Haus Wittgenstein (Bulgarian Cultural Institute): state-funded: the Bulgarian state owns the house and runs it as part of its embassy
funding: The institute says the Bulgarian government bought the house in 1975 and decided to make it a cultural institute that complements the embassy's work.

Bulgaria's and Austria's culture ministries supported the exhibition "Ludwig Wittgenstein: A Home for Gretl", opened on 28 November 2024 as a project of Austria's Wittgenstein Initiative; no amounts given (BTA).
details.bottom_line: The money is a foreign state's: Bulgaria owns and runs the house, with culture ministry backing for the 2024 exhibition. The weak points are the absence of any budget or accounts and the sale history, which rests on the institute's own account and on two Wikipedia versions that disagree on when Katlein bought (1968 or 1971). Worth watching: who pays for the upkeep of a protected monument, on which no reporting was found.

name: Kunstraum Dornbirn
funding: City of Dornbirn, Land Vorarlberg and the federal state, plus members and unnamed sponsors.
records_note: Lists its six-member managing board but shows sponsors as undated logos and posts no annual report or accounts.

overview: Contemporary art venue in the Stadtgarten park of Dornbirn, Vorarlberg, at Jahngasse 9. Its office is at Marktstraße 33.
Founded in 1987 as a private non-profit organisation to present and communicate contemporary art. It has used the historic assembly hall since 2003 (stated by the space).

The hall was built in 1893 by the Dornbirn turbine maker Rüschwerke to assemble its large turbine wheels. The company closed in 1984. Around 1999 and 2000 the industrial site was remodelled into the municipal Stadtgarten, and the assembly hall was left unchanged (stated by the space).
The brick hall measures 30 by 14 metres, 11.15 metres high, with about 350 square metres of exhibition space. It is not heatable (stated by the space).

It holds up to four exhibitions a year by established international artists and emerging ones. The current shows are Michail Pirgelis, "HYLE" (3 July to 8 November 2026), and Ursula Palla, "Pale Light" (20 November 2026 to 28 February 2027). It also runs education programmes, guided tours and a friends membership.
A six-member managing board runs it: Dr. Gerald A. Matt (President), Roland Jörg, Judith Berger-Neustädter, Peter Rhomberg, Dr. Sylvia Volz and Uli Zumtobel.

Visiting: open Tuesday to Sunday 10:00 to 18:00, closed Monday except public holidays. Admission is 4 euros for adults and 6.50 euros for families. Free for under 19s, students and apprentices, people with disabilities and friends of the Kunstraum.
details.funding_verdict: Kunstraum Dornbirn: supported by the City of Dornbirn, the Province of Vorarlberg, the Republic of Austria and Dornbirner Sparkasse
funding: The space states that it is supported by the City of Dornbirn, the Province of Vorarlberg, the Republic of Austria and Dornbirner Sparkasse (organisation page).

Long-standing partners thanked by name: inatura Dornbirn (ticketing network and community in the Stadtgarten), Studio Stefan Amann (communications and catalogues), Roland Adlassnigg's Atelier für außergewöhnliche Angelegenheiten (installations) and Günter Richard Wett (photography and film).
details.bottom_line: It is a private non-profit association founded in 1987.

name: Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Zentrum
funding: Verein Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Club is funded by Stadt Wien, Bezirk Margareten, the federal arts ministry, GESIBA and arching. ORF named Wertinvest, the building's owner, a financial backer in 2021.
watch: The architect's flat, open since October 2022. Wertinvest's Heumarkt tower put Vienna's historic centre on UNESCO's red list, 2017 to 2026.
why_flagged: The architect's flat, open since October 2022. Wertinvest's Heumarkt tower put Vienna's historic centre on UNESCO's red list, 2017 to 2026.
records_note: Names its funders and cooperation partners, with roles, on a page of its site.
affiliations_note: Run by Verein Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Club (ZVR 854118344), which ORF calls a publicly funded association. Member of Iconic Houses since December 2022.

overview: Museum in the architect's flat at Franzensgasse 16/40 in Vienna's 5th district (schuette-lihotzky.at).
Named for the architect Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky, who lived in the flat for about 30 years, moving in at age 70, and died in 2000 (ORF Wien).
ORF Wien reported in spring 2021 that the flat would open as a museum from autumn with weekly visits. The Zentrum has belonged to the "Iconic Houses" network since December 2022.

Flat of 55 square metres with a 35 square metre terrace. The bathroom tiles are original, the living room has furniture designed by her husband, and the original kitchen was to replace the current one (ORF Wien).
Also runs the research project "Architektur Pionierinnen", podcasts, readings and a film evening with VHS Wiener Urania since 2017 (schuette-lihotzky.at).
Visiting: Tuesday and Friday 14:00 to 18:00. Groups register by email.
details.funding_verdict: Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Zentrum: mainly public, plus the building owner Wertinvest
funding: The site lists these funders, with no roles or amounts: Bundeskammer der ZiviltechnikerInnen, the federal arts ministry (Bundesministerium für Kunst, Kultur, öffentlichen Dienst und Sport), the Stadt Wien culture department (MA 7), Bezirk Margareten and Gesiba.

ORF Wien reported in spring 2021 that the project is financially supported "unter anderem" by the house-owning company Wertinvest (my translation: among other backers). The site's cooperation page does not list Wertinvest.

red_flags.heading: Wertinvest and its owner Michael Tojner
points: Heumarkt: Vienna's historic centre was on UNESCO's Red List from 2017 because of Tojner's Heumarkt project; the World Heritage Committee removed it on 27 July 2026 although ICOMOS had recommended keeping it on. The plan fell from a 73-metre tower to 49.95 metres and still needs an environmental impact assessment (vienna.at).

Investigation: the anti-corruption prosecutor investigates Tojner, 15 other people and eight companies after a complaint from Land Burgenland about three housing companies losing non-profit status, with about EUR 40 million of alleged damage; Tojner's lawyer rejects all accusations (ORF Wien, June 2019). Industriemagazin counts 16 individuals and nine companies.

Unverified: Greens club chairman David Ellensohn alleged in 2018 that Tojner and managers of Urbanauts Hospitality rented non-profit flats to tourists above the legal rent, from ORF Wien; the source is a party complaint. Wertinvest said Ellensohn was trying to make political capital and called its arrangement "rechtlich einwandfrei" (legally sound, my translation).

wider_context: Members of the Architekturinitiative Wien, including Friedrich Achleitner and Gustav Peichl, wrote to planning councillor Maria Vassilakou that the Heumarkt project took public space in breach of the competition brief and that a luxury residential tower could not be justified there (ORF Wien, April 2014, my translation).
ICOMOS, UNESCO's advisory body, recommended keeping Vienna on the Red List (vienna.at, 2026).
Wertinvest, which owns the Zentrum's building and backs the project, is the company behind the Heumarkt project.
details.bottom_line: The public money has no flagged funder found. The private backer is Wertinvest, whose owner Tojner is under investigation in the Burgenland case (denied) and whose Heumarkt project kept Vienna on UNESCO's Red List from 2017 to 2026. The weak points are the missing amounts and accounts and the dependence on the building's owner. Worth watching: the outcome of the Burgenland case and the Heumarkt environmental assessment.

name: Baku Museum of Modern Art
funding: Opened 20 Mar 2009 with about 800 works; founded by First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva and funded by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, which she heads.
watch: A ruling-family foundation is its only known funder; the director since 2012 is Aida Mahmudova, founder of YARAT.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: It carries only about, visit, library and what's-on pages.

overview: Museum of modern art at Yusif Safarov Street 5, Baku (Wikipedia).
Opened on 20 March 2009 at the initiative of First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva (Wikipedia).
Aida Mahmudova has been its director since 2012. She is also the founder of YARAT, the Baku contemporary art organisation (Wikipedia, Aida Mahmudova page).

Building: Wikipedia credits the artist Altay Sadigzade as chief designer and architect. The design avoids halls with corners and uses open passages and walls that meet at different angles, joined by metallic structures and the colour white.
Collection: over 800 works by Azerbaijani painters and sculptors, particularly avant-garde art of the 1960s and 1970s. Wikipedia adds works by Dalí, Picasso and Chagall from private collectors.

Wikipedia also describes a wider "eco-cultural zone" conceived by Thomas Krens, former Guggenheim Foundation director, and planned to include a Frank Gehry skyscraper and a walkway over the Caspian Sea.
details.funding_verdict: Baku Museum of Modern Art: funded by a ruling-family foundation: the Heydar Aliyev Foundation
funding: The Heydar Aliyev Foundation, which the First Lady heads, funded the museum (Wikipedia).
OCCRP describes the foundation as a non-governmental organisation set up and run by the family of President Ilham Aliyev (2015).
wider_context: OCCRP and its RISE Project partners (Roxana Jipa, Victor Ilie, Daniel Bojin, 4 December 2015): the Heydar Aliyev Foundation's Bucharest headquarters, a house that cost 6.5 million euros, is provided free of charge by the Romanian company Curzon Properties, whose owners are hidden behind offshore companies. The Seychelles company Asbet Ltd paid the full price. Asbet's majority stake passed in March 2009 to Ciaba Ltd, a British Virgin Islands company that documents obtained by OCCRP show was owned by Arzu Aliyeva, the president's younger daughter. The article is about the foundation and does not mention the museum.

Hyperallergic (Nevdon Jamgochian, "Artwashing a Dictatorship", 28 February 2021, https://hyperallergic.com/artwashing-a-dictatorship/): argues the Aliyev family uses art and cultural institutions to repair its international image. The author writes that YARAT is "almost certainly funded by the state" and that it is "impossible to see how this organization is funded in any way but through the Aliyevs", which is the author's own inference; the article says Mahmudova claimed an unnamed bank backs YARAT. It names Mahmudova as the dictator's niece who runs YARAT and does not name the Baku Museum of Modern Art.

The Art Newspaper (Anna Sansom, "Artist demands Baku art centre pulls his exhibition for using it as a 'propaganda tool' in Azerbaijan-Armenia conflict", 30 October 2020, https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2020/10/30/artist-demands-baku-art-centre-pulls-his-exhibition-for-using-it-as-a-propaganda-tool-in-azerbaijan-armenia-conflict): the artist Ahmet Ogut accused YARAT of using his exhibition banner as a propaganda tool; YARAT's website said the show closed on 28 October 2020, about three weeks early. The article is about YARAT and does not name the museum.
Hyperallergic (Dorian Batycka, 2 November 2020) calls Mahmudova, the founder of YARAT, the niece of Ilham Aliyev; Wikipedia calls her a niece of Mehriban Aliyeva.
Mahmudova, the founder of YARAT, has directed the Baku Museum of Modern Art since 2012 (Wikipedia, Aida Mahmudova page).
details.bottom_line: The museum's named funder is the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, a foundation set up and run by the family of President Ilham Aliyev and headed by the First Lady (Wikipedia, OCCRP). Its director, Aida Mahmudova, founded YARAT, which Hyperallergic and The Art Newspaper have covered.

name: RAK Art Foundation
funding: Private non-profit founded by Rashid Al Khalifa and housed in his family home with his collection.
records_note: The about page names only the founder Rashid Al Khalifa.
affiliations_note: RAK Art Foundation sends RAK Art Prize winners to a residency at The Art Station in Muharraq Souq, Bahrain.

overview: Non-profit art foundation in Riffa, in the centre of Bahrain, housed in the restored childhood home of its founder, Rashid Al Khalifa (Identity, Lemma Shehadi, 15 June 2022).

Founder Rashid Al Khalifa, born in Riffa in 1952, is an artist, patron and collector who founded the Bahrain Arts Society in 1983 (foundation website). Identity describes him as a member of the Bahraini royal family.
Launched in 2020 as the Rashid Al Khalifa Art Foundation (Identity). The foundation's own site says a white-cube gallery extension was completed in 2020.

The house dates from the 1920s with a 1960s extension that includes his childhood bedroom. He acquired it from his family in 2014 and restored and expanded it with Italian architect Davide Chiaverini, adding a two-storey courtyard pavilion with steel mashrabiya panels (Identity).

The collection holds hundreds of international works of fine and decorative art (foundation website), including Pierre Soulages, Damien Hirst, Fernando Botero, Mohammed Melehi and Fateh Al Moudarres, and Al Khalifa's own work (Identity).

The foundation's site lists exhibitions, the RAK Art Prize and The Art Station as its programmes. Bahrain Confidential states that Shaikh Rashid bin Khalifa Al Khalifa founded it in Riffa to make an enormous art collection available to the Bahraini people (Bahrain Confidential, 14 May 2025).

The Art Station ran a three-month residency in Bahrain from 7 March to 30 May 2024 for US citizens over 21, with housing, a monthly stipend of 1,500 USD and a 5,300 USD artwork production grant (e-flux announcement, 20 January 2024).
details.funding_verdict: RAK Art Foundation: founder-led non-profit; one documented outside grant, from the US Embassy
funding: The foundation's own site describes it as a non-profit. It occupies the founder's childhood home, which he acquired from his family in 2014 (foundation website, Identity).
The 2024 Art Station residency was "funded by the US Embassy in Manama" (e-flux announcement).
not_related: Ras Al Khaimah Art (RAK Art) in the United Arab Emirates. The Al Qasimi Foundation's arts and culture page says the Ras Al Khaimah Art Festival was founded in 2013 and is now Ras Al Khaimah Art, a year-round hub, and that the Al Qasimi Foundation convenes the community through the annual festival and funds its Artist-in-Residence Program and Film Grants. It is a different organisation from the Bahrain foundation, which is based in Riffa and founded by Rashid Al Khalifa; the two share only the abbreviation "RAK" (Al Qasimi Foundation, Ras Al Khaimah Art website).
details.bottom_line: The RAK Art Foundation is a non-profit built around one collector's collection and childhood home in Riffa, Bahrain. The documented outside money is the US Embassy in Manama's funding of the 2024 Art Station residency.

name: Bengal Foundation
funding: Private trust founded in 1986, funded entirely by the Bengal Group. Chairman Abul Khair Litu co-founded AB Bank. It runs a fine arts gallery, a music festival and publishing.
watch: In July 2024 the Anti-Corruption Commission endorsed a charge sheet against Litu for acquiring about Tk 903 million in assets beyond his income.
why_flagged: In July 2024 the Anti-Corruption Commission endorsed a charge sheet against Litu for acquiring about Tk 903 million in assets beyond his income.
records_note: Names its Board of Trustees and says the trustees fund it.
affiliations_note: Lists the Bengal Shilpalaya, S M Sultan Bengal Art College and Bengal Parampara Sangeetalay as units, and has worked with the National Crafts Council of Bangladesh for a decade.

overview: Non-profit cultural trust headquartered at Bengal Shilpalay in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, that stages exhibitions, concerts and publishing.
Founded in 1986 by industrialist Abul Khair Litu, its chairman, to "promote and showcase Bangladeshi art on a larger platform" (Wikipedia).

Bengal Shilpalay began in 2000 with a solo show by Mohammad Kibria and reopened in April 2019 as a renovated, museum-like space with halls named for Quamrul Hassan and Subir Choudhury. Khair said it would no longer run commercial operations (The Daily Star).

Since 1999 it has run international art camps with nearly 300 artists. It also runs Bengal Publications, which issues books, magazines and folios, and the Bengal Classical Music Festival, which it calls the world's largest classical music festival in performers on a single stage, audience capacity and duration (stated by the space).
details.funding_verdict: Bengal Foundation: family company money: a private trust funded by Abul Khair Litu's Bengal Group
funding: Registered as a private trust and "funded entirely by the Bengal Group" (Wikipedia).
Litu chairs Bengal Group Ltd., co-founded AB Bank, Bangladesh's first private bank, in 1981, and chairs the Bengal Institute for Architecture, Landscapes and Settlements (Bengal Institute).

red_flags.heading: Corruption case against the founder
points: The Anti-Corruption Commission approved a charge sheet in July 2024 against Litu, chairman of Bengal Group Limited, for acquiring illegal assets of over Tk 903 million beyond his known income and hiding over Tk 1.24 million in his asset declaration (The Financial Express).
The ACC case was filed on 23 April 2017; he was questioned on 1 November 2017 over bank embezzlement and tax evasion (The Financial Express).
The ACC also found Tk 25.26 million in illegal assets beyond the known income of his wife, Mahua Khair (The Financial Express).
In June 2007 a Dhaka court sent Litu, then Bengal Group chairman, to Dhaka Central Jail on 30 days' detention after his three-day remand expired (The Daily Star).

not_related: Bengal Group of Industries, the Dhaka conglomerate behind Bengal Plastic and RTV, founded in 1969 by Morshed Alam, who chairs it. Its Wikipedia page does not mention Litu or the foundation; Litu's company is Bengal Group Ltd.
details.bottom_line: The foundation runs on one family company's money with no published accounts. The weak point is its founder and funder, charged in 2024 with holding Tk 903 million in assets beyond his known income. Worth watching: the outcome of the ACC case and whether the foundation ever publishes accounts.

name: Art-Siadziba
watch: Founded 24 December 2011. Evicted several times. At Instrumentalny lane 6 from October 2013. On the liquidation list in July 2021. Ended activities January 2022.
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
records_note: Art-Siadziba was a Minsk non-profit portal liquidated in July 2021.

overview: Independent cultural platform in Minsk that promoted the Belarusian language through concerts, lectures and entertainment events for young people (Radio Svaboda).

Founded on 24 December 2011. Radio Svaboda names Pavel Belavus as founder and first director. Wikipedia lists Stas Babaytsau, Franak Viachorka and Zmicier Afanasenka as founders. Kalektar names Belavus as founder and Afanasenka and Viachorka as co-founders.
The English Wikipedia entry translates the name as "Art Headquarters".

Venues: the Horizont factory building, then 28a Pushkin Avenue, then a two-room flat in central Minsk and, from 2013, 6 Instrumentalny Lane (Kalektar). A new space planned for 4 Maskvin Lane was lost in December 2012 before it opened (Nasha Niva, 6 December 2012).
Programme: concerts, presentations and film screenings (Nasha Niva, December 2012), book launches and lectures (Nasha Niva, July 2012).
It announced on 3 January 2022 that it was ending its activity (Radio Svaboda).
details.funding_verdict: Art-Siadziba: independent venue in rented premises, with a 2014 crowdfunding appeal for a building of its own
funding: In 2014 the "Dom" (House) campaign raised a little over $4,000 in 10 days toward a goal of $200,000, sold as 40,000 virtual bricks at $5 each (Charter97, 6 March 2014).

Premises were rented: the planned Maskvin Lane space belonged to JSC Sukno and was leased by JSC RefOilProdukt, with Art-Siadziba as sub-tenant (Nasha Niva, 6 December 2012); at Instrumentalny Lane the owner was the Belarusian Society of Hunters and Fishermen, which let Art-Siadziba stay until 1 May 2014 (Charter97, 6 March 2014).
wider_context: Radio Svaboda reports that by the end of 2021 the Belarusian authorities had liquidated at least 275 non-governmental organisations, with more in liquidation or under threat. An update on the same page says that in July 2022 it became known that 857 had been liquidated or driven to self-liquidation.

Amnesty International (Aisha Jung, 22 February 2021): "The authorities are methodically destroying Belarus's spirited cultural life and its most creative members." The statement is about the country's cultural scene as a whole.
In July 2012, when the space had closed for the first time, the city culture department told Nasha Niva it does not handle decisions of this kind.

Unverified: after the third loss of premises in December 2012, Pavel Belavus said the landlord was summoned to the Minsk City Executive Committee and strongly advised to cancel the lease, and that the order came from its ideology department; Nasha Niva reports this as Belavus's account.

Radio Svaboda reports that it was placed on a list of organisations subject to liquidation in late July 2021 and announced on 3 January 2022 that it was ending its activity. Belavus faced a criminal case under Article 342 of the Criminal Code and was held in SIZO-1 in Minsk when Svaboda published.
details.bottom_line: Art-Siadziba was an independent venue in rented premises, with a 2014 crowdfunding appeal for a building of its own. It was placed on a liquidation list in July 2021 and ended its activity in January 2022, during the wider Belarusian liquidation of non-governmental organisations.
